_about: Biomarkers: the individual substances the tests measure. Each page explains what the marker is, which organ makes or clears it, why a result may be higher or lower and what can distort it. Reference intervals belong to the laboratory that ran the test; nothing here interprets an individual result.

haemoglobin.name: Haemoglobin
haemoglobin.summary: The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue. Its concentration is the standard measure of anaemia and the first number read on a full blood count.
haemoglobin.what: Each red cell is packed with haemoglobin, a four-part protein whose iron atoms bind oxygen in the lung capillaries and release it where oxygen is low. The concentration in blood reflects the balance between production in the bone marrow (which needs iron, vitamin B12, folate and the kidney hormone erythropoietin) and loss or destruction of red cells. A low value is anaemia; the size of the red cells (MCV) then points to the cause.
haemoglobin.unit: g/L in the UK, g/dL in the United States (1 g/dL = 10 g/L)
higher: Living at altitude, smoking and chronic lung disease (the body makes more red cells when oxygen is scarce)
Dehydration, which concentrates the blood
Polycythaemia vera and other bone-marrow disorders
Testosterone and erythropoietin treatment
lower: Blood loss: heavy periods, bleeding from the gut, surgery or injury
Iron, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Chronic kidney disease (too little erythropoietin) and long-term inflammatory disease
Haemolysis, inherited haemoglobin disorders (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease), bone-marrow failure
Pregnancy, where plasma volume expands faster than red-cell mass
factors: Pregnancy and the menstrual cycle
Fluid balance at the time of sampling
Recent transfusion or blood donation
Sex, age and altitude of residence, which change the reference interval
haemoglobin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

haematocrit.name: Haematocrit
haematocrit.summary: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells, reported as a percentage or a ratio. It tracks haemoglobin closely and is part of every full blood count.
haematocrit.what: Spin a tube of blood and the red cells settle into a packed column; the height of that column as a share of the whole is the haematocrit. Automated analysers calculate it from the red-cell count and their average size. Because red cells carry the haemoglobin, haematocrit and haemoglobin rise and fall together, and the ratio between them (the MCHC) is one of the red-cell indices. Haematocrit also sets blood viscosity: very high values make blood thicker and harder to pump.
higher: Dehydration and burns (loss of plasma water)
Chronic hypoxia: lung disease, smoking, altitude, cyanotic heart disease
Polycythaemia vera
Erythropoietin or testosterone use
lower: Any cause of anaemia: iron, B12 or folate deficiency, blood loss, haemolysis, marrow failure, chronic disease
Over-hydration or large volumes of intravenous fluid
Pregnancy (dilution)
factors: Fluid intake and dehydration
Posture and tourniquet time during sampling
Pregnancy
Altitude
haematocrit.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

mcv.name: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
mcv.summary: The average size of a red blood cell, calculated by the analyser during a full blood count. Small cells (microcytosis) point towards iron deficiency, large cells (macrocytosis) towards B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol or liver disease.
mcv.what: Red cells are normally about 80 to 100 femtolitres in volume. When haemoglobin production is limited by iron shortage or a thalassaemia trait, the marrow releases smaller, paler cells. When DNA synthesis is slowed by lack of vitamin B12 or folate, or by alcohol, some drugs or liver disease, cells are released larger than normal. The MCV is therefore the first branch point in working out why someone is anaemic, alongside the red cell distribution width (RDW), which measures how variable the sizes are.
higher: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Alcohol excess and liver disease
Hypothyroidism
Some medicines (for example hydroxycarbamide, methotrexate, some antiretrovirals)
Reticulocytosis after bleeding or haemolysis (young red cells are large)
Myelodysplasia
lower: Iron deficiency
Thalassaemia trait and other inherited haemoglobin disorders
Long-standing inflammatory disease (anaemia of chronic disease, sometimes)
Lead poisoning (rare)
factors: A mixed deficiency (iron and B12) can leave the MCV normal
Recent transfusion
Very high white-cell counts or cold agglutinins can distort analyser readings
mcv.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

white-cell-count.name: White blood cell count
white-cell-count.summary: The total number of white blood cells in a volume of blood: the immune cells that fight infection and drive inflammation. The differential then splits the total into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.
white-cell-count.what: White cells are made in the bone marrow and travel through blood to the tissues where they work. The count rises quickly when the marrow releases stored neutrophils in response to bacterial infection, tissue injury, steroids or stress, and falls when the marrow is suppressed, when cells are consumed faster than they are made, or in some viral infections. The total count on its own is only a starting point: the differential says which cell line has changed, and a blood film shows what the cells look like.
white-cell-count.unit: ×10⁹/L (cells per litre); the same number as thousands per microlitre in US units
higher: Bacterial infection and sepsis (mostly neutrophils)
Inflammation, tissue damage, burns, heart attack
Corticosteroid treatment, smoking, stress and heavy exercise
Leukaemia and other bone-marrow disorders
After the spleen is removed
lower: Viral infections, including influenza and HIV
Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and some medicines (for example clozapine, carbimazole, methotrexate)
Bone-marrow failure or infiltration
Severe sepsis (consumption), some autoimmune diseases, B12 or folate deficiency
A normal variant in some people of African or Middle Eastern ancestry (benign ethnic neutropenia)
factors: Time of day, exercise, smoking and pregnancy
Recent steroid or adrenaline-type medicines
Sample clumping or delays can give a spurious count
white-cell-count.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

neutrophils.name: Neutrophils
neutrophils.summary: The most numerous white blood cell and the first responder to bacterial infection. The absolute neutrophil count from the differential is the number clinicians use to judge infection risk during chemotherapy and to recognise a bacterial cause of illness.
neutrophils.what: Neutrophils are short-lived cells that leave the marrow, circulate for hours and then move into tissues to engulf and kill bacteria and fungi. The marrow keeps a large reserve that can be released within hours, which is why the count climbs so fast in bacterial infection, after injury and with corticosteroids. A very low count (neutropenia) leaves the body open to serious infection: a fever in someone with a count below about 0.5 ×10⁹/L is treated as an emergency (neutropenic sepsis).
higher: Bacterial infection, abscess, sepsis
Tissue injury: surgery, burns, heart attack, gout flares
Corticosteroids, lithium, colony-stimulating factors
Smoking, stress, strenuous exercise, pregnancy and labour
Chronic myeloid leukaemia and other myeloproliferative disorders
lower: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Medicines such as clozapine, carbimazole, sulfasalazine, methotrexate
Overwhelming sepsis, viral infections
Bone-marrow failure, B12 or folate deficiency
Autoimmune neutropenia; benign ethnic neutropenia
factors: Exercise and adrenaline release shift cells from vessel walls into the circulation for a short time
Time since a steroid dose
Ethnic background changes the reference interval
neutrophils.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

lymphocytes.name: Lymphocytes
lymphocytes.summary: The white blood cells of adaptive immunity: B cells that make antibodies, T cells that direct the response and kill infected cells, and natural killer cells. The lymphocyte count rises in many viral infections and falls with steroids, HIV and some cancers.
lymphocytes.what: Lymphocytes circulate between blood, lymph nodes, the spleen and the tissues, and most of them are outside the bloodstream at any moment. In children the normal count is much higher than in adults. A high count is common in viral infections such as glandular fever and in whooping cough; a persistently high count in an older adult raises the question of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. A low count is seen with corticosteroids, acute illness, HIV infection, some autoimmune diseases and after chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
higher: Viral infections (glandular fever, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis, many childhood viruses)
Whooping cough, tuberculosis, brucellosis
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoma
Smoking; after removal of the spleen
lower: Corticosteroids and acute stress or illness
HIV infection
Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunosuppressants
Lupus, kidney failure, severe sepsis, malnutrition
Bone-marrow failure
factors: Age: children run much higher counts
A recent viral illness can leave the count changed for weeks
Steroid dose timing
lymphocytes.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

platelets.name: Platelets
platelets.summary: Small cell fragments that plug damaged vessel walls and start the clotting cascade. Too few (thrombocytopenia) and the person bruises and bleeds; too many (thrombocytosis) is usually a reaction to inflammation, bleeding or iron deficiency.
platelets.what: Platelets bud off from giant marrow cells called megakaryocytes and survive for about 7 to 10 days, with a third held in the spleen. When a vessel is injured they stick to the exposed wall, activate, clump together and provide the surface on which clotting factors assemble. The count is part of the full blood count. Bleeding from a low count usually appears as pinpoint spots (petechiae), bruises, nosebleeds and gum bleeding; spontaneous serious bleeding becomes a risk below about 20 ×10⁹/L. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin change how platelets work without changing the count.
higher: Reactive: infection, inflammation, surgery, bleeding, iron deficiency, cancer
After the spleen is removed
Essential thrombocythaemia and other myeloproliferative disorders
lower: Immune thrombocytopenia (antibodies destroy platelets)
Medicines: heparin, some antibiotics, chemotherapy, sodium valproate, alcohol
Liver disease and an enlarged spleen (platelets pooled in the spleen)
Bone-marrow failure, B12 or folate deficiency, leukaemia
Sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, pregnancy (mild), some viral infections
factors: Platelets can clump in the tube and read falsely low (pseudothrombocytopenia): a repeat in a different tube or a blood film settles it
Recent surgery, infection or iron deficiency raises the count
Pregnancy lowers it slightly
platelets.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

hba1c.name: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin)
hba1c.summary: Haemoglobin that has glucose attached to it. Because red cells live about three months, the HbA1c fraction reports average blood glucose over the previous two to three months and is the marker used to diagnose and monitor type 2 diabetes.
hba1c.what: Glucose in the blood attaches to haemoglobin slowly and irreversibly, so the higher the average glucose, the larger the share of haemoglobin that is glycated. Because the red cell population turns over every 120 days or so, HbA1c averages glucose exposure across that period, with the most recent month weighing most. It is reported in mmol/mol (the IFCC standard used in the UK) or as a percentage (the older DCCT units used in the United States). Unlike a single glucose reading it does not need fasting and is not disturbed by what was eaten that morning.
higher: Sustained high blood glucose: diabetes or prediabetes
Iron deficiency anaemia and other states with older red cells (falsely high)
Kidney failure, some haemoglobin variants (assay-dependent)
lower: Recent blood loss, haemolysis or transfusion (younger red cells: falsely low)
Pregnancy, erythropoietin treatment, some haemoglobin variants
Improving glucose control
factors: Any condition that shortens or lengthens red-cell survival changes the value independently of glucose
Haemoglobin variants can interfere with some assay methods
It cannot show day-to-day swings or hypoglycaemia
hba1c.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

glucose.name: Blood glucose
glucose.summary: The concentration of glucose, the body's main circulating fuel, in blood at the moment of sampling. Kept within narrow limits by insulin and glucagon, it rises after meals and in diabetes and falls dangerously in hypoglycaemia.
glucose.what: Glucose enters blood from the gut after meals and from the liver between them; insulin from the pancreas moves it into muscle and fat and switches off liver production, while glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise it. A fasting sample, a random sample and a sample two hours after a measured glucose drink each answer a different question, which is why the timing must be recorded with the result. Laboratories measure plasma glucose from a fluoride tube; fingerprick meters and continuous monitors estimate it from capillary blood or tissue fluid and read slightly differently.
higher: Diabetes and prediabetes
Acute illness, infection, heart attack, surgery (stress hyperglycaemia)
Corticosteroids and some other medicines
Cushing syndrome, pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer
lower: Too much insulin or a sulfonylurea relative to food and activity
Alcohol, especially without food
Severe liver disease, adrenal insufficiency, sepsis
Insulin-producing tumours (rare); reactive hypoglycaemia after gastric surgery
factors: Time since the last meal or drink and what it contained
Exercise, illness, stress and sleep
A delay between sampling and analysis lowers the value unless a fluoride tube is used
Meter readings differ from laboratory plasma values
glucose.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

troponin.name: Cardiac troponin
troponin.summary: A protein of the contractile apparatus of heart muscle cells that leaks into blood when those cells are injured. High-sensitivity troponin is the blood marker that rules a heart attack in or out, read as a change between two samples a few hours apart.
troponin.what: Troponin I and troponin T are parts of the machinery that lets calcium trigger contraction in heart muscle; the cardiac forms are distinct from those in skeletal muscle, so the assay is specific to the heart. When cardiac cells die, troponin appears in blood within a few hours, peaks around a day and can stay raised for one to two weeks. Modern high-sensitivity assays detect tiny amounts in almost everyone, so the diagnosis of acute injury rests on a value above the assay's 99th percentile together with a rise or fall between serial samples, interpreted with symptoms and the ECG. Injury is not the same as infarction: pulmonary embolism, sepsis, myocarditis, kidney failure, very fast heart rhythms and extreme exertion all release troponin without a blocked coronary artery.
troponin.unit: ng/L; every assay has its own 99th-percentile upper reference limit, so numbers are not comparable between hospitals
higher: Acute myocardial infarction (with a rise or fall on serial samples)
Myocarditis, pericarditis, heart failure, takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary embolism, sepsis, severe respiratory failure
Tachyarrhythmias, cardiac procedures, cardioversion, chest trauma
Chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance) and structural heart disease (stable, flat elevation)
lower: A low value is expected; an undetectable high-sensitivity result on arrival, hours after symptom onset, makes acute infarction very unlikely
factors: Time since symptom onset: a single early sample can be normal before the rise
Kidney function
Assay type and its 99th percentile; laboratory-specific sex-specific limits
Very rarely, antibodies in the sample interfere with the assay
troponin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

bnp.name: Natriuretic peptides (BNP and NT-proBNP)
bnp.summary: Hormones released by the heart's ventricles when their walls are stretched by high pressure or volume. A normal level makes heart failure unlikely; a high level in someone breathless calls for an echocardiogram and specialist assessment.
bnp.what: Ventricular muscle cells make pro-BNP and split it into active BNP and the inactive fragment NT-proBNP; laboratories measure one or the other, and the two have different reference limits. BNP acts on the kidney to shed sodium and water and relaxes blood vessels, a natural counterweight to the fluid retention of heart failure. Because release is proportional to wall stress, the level rises with heart failure of either reduced or preserved ejection fraction, with valve disease, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary embolism. Guidelines use NT-proBNP bands to decide how urgently a person with suspected heart failure should be seen for echocardiography.
bnp.unit: ng/L (pg/mL) for both peptides; BNP and NT-proBNP have separate thresholds and are not interchangeable
higher: Heart failure of any cause, valve disease, myocardial infarction
Atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension
Chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance), sepsis, older age
Left ventricular hypertrophy, some chemotherapy
lower: Obesity lowers the level, which can mask heart failure
Treatment with diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and sacubitril/valsartan changes levels (sacubitril raises BNP but not NT-proBNP)
factors: Age, kidney function and body weight
Whether the laboratory measures BNP or NT-proBNP
Acute illness on the day of sampling
bnp.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

total-cholesterol.name: Total cholesterol
total-cholesterol.summary: The sum of all the cholesterol carried in blood by lipoproteins: LDL, HDL and the remainder. One line of a lipid profile, useful mainly as the starting point for the ratios and the non-HDL value that guide cardiovascular risk assessment.
total-cholesterol.what: Cholesterol is a waxy molecule every cell needs for its membranes and for making steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. It does not dissolve in water, so it travels in blood packaged with proteins as lipoproteins. The total is dominated by LDL cholesterol, the fraction deposited in artery walls, and HDL cholesterol, the fraction being carried back to the liver. A high total is therefore not always harmful (a large HDL share is protective) and a normal total can hide a poor pattern, which is why risk calculators use the ratio of total to HDL and guidelines increasingly track non-HDL cholesterol instead.
higher: Diet high in saturated fat, excess weight, inactivity
Familial hypercholesterolaemia and other inherited lipid disorders
Hypothyroidism, kidney disease with heavy proteinuria, cholestatic liver disease
Pregnancy; some medicines (corticosteroids, some antiretrovirals, isotretinoin)
lower: Hyperthyroidism, malnutrition, malabsorption
Severe acute illness, cancer, advanced liver disease
Lipid-lowering treatment
factors: Acute illness, surgery and heart attack lower cholesterol for several weeks
Weight change, alcohol and pregnancy
Fasting is no longer required for most purposes but changes triglycerides more than cholesterol
total-cholesterol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

ldl-cholesterol.name: LDL cholesterol
ldl-cholesterol.summary: The cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein, the particle that deposits cholesterol in artery walls and drives atherosclerosis. The main target of statin treatment and the lipid value most closely tied to heart attack and stroke risk.
ldl-cholesterol.what: The liver packages triglycerides and cholesterol into VLDL particles; as tissues strip out the triglyceride, the particles shrink into cholesterol-rich LDL. LDL delivers cholesterol to cells through LDL receptors, but when particles are numerous or the artery wall is damaged they enter the wall, are oxidised and are engulfed by macrophages that become the foam cells of a fatty plaque. Statins lower LDL by making the liver display more LDL receptors. Laboratories usually calculate LDL from total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides (the Friedewald equation), which becomes unreliable when triglycerides are high; non-HDL cholesterol (total minus HDL) avoids that problem and is the value UK guidance uses for treatment targets.
ldl-cholesterol.unit: mmol/L (UK) or mg/dL (US); usually calculated rather than measured directly
higher: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (very high levels from childhood, often with family history of early heart disease)
Saturated-fat-rich diet, obesity, inactivity
Hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, diabetes
Some medicines (corticosteroids, ciclosporin, some antipsychotics)
lower: Lipid-lowering treatment (statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors)
Hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, severe illness, advanced liver disease
Rare inherited disorders of lipoprotein synthesis
factors: Very high triglycerides make the calculated LDL invalid
Acute illness lowers the level for weeks
Fasting state changes the triglyceride input to the calculation
ldl-cholesterol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

NICE CG71: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: identification and management

hdl-cholesterol.name: HDL cholesterol
hdl-cholesterol.summary: The cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein, the particle that collects cholesterol from tissues and artery walls and returns it to the liver. A higher level is associated with lower cardiovascular risk and enters the standard risk calculators.
hdl-cholesterol.what: HDL particles are made by the liver and gut and pick up cholesterol from peripheral cells, including the foam cells of a developing plaque, delivering it back to the liver for excretion in bile (reverse cholesterol transport). Population studies show a steady fall in heart disease as HDL rises, so it appears in risk scores such as QRISK as the total-to-HDL ratio. Drugs that raise HDL have not, however, reduced heart attacks in trials, so HDL is read as a risk marker rather than a treatment target. Exercise, weight loss, stopping smoking and moderate alcohol raise it; obesity, inactivity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and high triglycerides lower it.
higher: Regular aerobic exercise, moderate alcohol intake, oestrogen
Some inherited traits (usually harmless); very high values with some genetic variants are of uncertain significance
lower: Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking
Type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides, metabolic syndrome
Anabolic steroids, some beta blockers and progestogens
Rare inherited HDL deficiencies
factors: Recent alcohol, weight change and exercise habits
Acute illness
Menopause and hormone treatment
hdl-cholesterol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

triglycerides.name: Triglycerides
triglycerides.summary: The main form in which fat is stored and transported: three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone, carried in blood by chylomicrons after meals and by VLDL from the liver. Raised levels add to cardiovascular risk and very high levels can trigger pancreatitis.
triglycerides.what: After a fatty meal the gut packages triglyceride into chylomicrons, which is why a non-fasting sample reads higher and why laboratories once insisted on fasting. Between meals the liver exports triglyceride in VLDL, particularly when it is over-supplied with calories, alcohol or sugar, or when insulin resistance lets fat stores release fatty acids freely. Moderately raised triglycerides usually travel with low HDL, central obesity and prediabetes; levels above about 10 mmol/L carry a real risk of acute pancreatitis. Because triglyceride-rich particles contribute to non-HDL cholesterol, the lipid profile as a whole rather than the single number guides treatment.
higher: A recent meal, alcohol, sugary and refined-carbohydrate-rich diets
Obesity, type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome
Hypothyroidism, kidney disease, pregnancy
Medicines: corticosteroids, oestrogens, isotretinoin, some antipsychotics, thiazides, beta blockers
Inherited hypertriglyceridaemia (familial chylomicronaemia, familial combined hyperlipidaemia)
lower: Malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism
Fibrates, omega-3 preparations, statins to a lesser degree, weight loss
factors: Fasting versus non-fasting sampling (up to a few hours' difference)
Alcohol in the preceding days
Acute illness and pregnancy
triglycerides.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification

alt.name: ALT (alanine aminotransferase)
alt.summary: An enzyme concentrated in liver cells that leaks into blood when they are injured. The most liver-specific of the routine liver blood tests and the one that rises first in fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis and drug-induced injury.
alt.what: ALT sits in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes, where it shuttles amino groups between amino acids as part of energy metabolism. Damage to the cell membrane releases it into the circulation, so the level rises with hepatocellular injury of any cause: viral hepatitis, alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, drugs and toxins, or a congested liver in heart failure. Because ALT is mostly confined to the liver it is more specific than AST, and the ratio between the two helps distinguish alcohol-related disease (AST higher) from other causes (ALT higher). A mildly raised ALT is common and often reflects fatty liver; a level many times the upper limit points to acute hepatitis, ischaemia or paracetamol toxicity.
alt.unit: U/L (units per litre); reference limits differ by laboratory and sex
higher: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes
Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E), glandular fever
Alcohol; medicines such as paracetamol in overdose, statins, antibiotics, antiepileptics, methotrexate
Autoimmune hepatitis, haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, coeliac disease
Ischaemic liver injury, heart failure with congestion, bile-duct obstruction (with ALP)
Strenuous exercise and muscle injury (smaller effect than on AST)
lower: A low value has little clinical meaning; vitamin B6 deficiency and advanced cirrhosis with few remaining hepatocytes can lower it
factors: Recent strenuous exercise, alcohol and new medicines
Body weight and sex change the reference interval
Haemolysed samples
Time of day (slightly higher in the afternoon)
alt.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

ast.name: AST (aspartate aminotransferase)
ast.summary: An enzyme found in liver cells but also in heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, brain and red cells. It rises with liver injury alongside ALT, and the AST:ALT ratio helps point towards or away from alcohol-related liver disease.
ast.what: AST is present both in the cytoplasm and in the mitochondria of cells, and it is far less specific to the liver than ALT. In hepatocellular injury both enzymes rise; in alcohol-related liver disease AST is typically higher than ALT (a ratio above 2), partly because alcohol depletes the vitamin B6 that ALT needs and damages mitochondria. Muscle injury, a heart attack, haemolysis and vigorous exercise all raise AST with little change in ALT, so an isolated AST elevation prompts a creatine kinase test. In advanced fibrosis the ratio flips because ALT production falls, which is why AST-based scores (such as APRI and FIB-4) are used to estimate scarring.
higher: All causes of hepatocellular injury: hepatitis, fatty liver, drugs, alcohol, ischaemia
Alcohol-related liver disease (AST greater than ALT)
Muscle disease or injury, rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise, seizures
Heart attack, haemolysis, pancreatitis, coeliac disease
Cirrhosis with advanced fibrosis (AST:ALT ratio rises)
lower: Low values are not clinically important; chronic kidney disease and B6 deficiency can lower them
factors: Exercise in the preceding days, intramuscular injections, muscle bruising
Haemolysed samples read falsely high
Alcohol intake and medicines
ast.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

alp.name: ALP (alkaline phosphatase)
alp.summary: An enzyme made mainly by the cells lining the bile ducts and by bone-forming cells. A raised level with a raised GGT points to obstructed bile flow (cholestasis); a raised level with a normal GGT points to bone, growth or pregnancy.
alp.what: Alkaline phosphatase is anchored to the membranes of bile-duct cells, osteoblasts in bone, the placenta and the gut lining. When bile flow is obstructed, by a gallstone in the common bile duct, a tumour of the pancreas head or bile ducts, or by drugs that impair bile secretion, the liver makes far more ALP and releases it into blood. Growing children and adolescents have naturally high bone ALP, as do people healing a fracture, and the placenta raises it in the third trimester of pregnancy. Distinguishing liver from bone ALP relies on the GGT (raised only in the liver pattern) or on measuring the separate isoenzymes.
alp.unit: U/L (units per litre); much higher in growing children
higher: Cholestasis: bile-duct stones, strictures, pancreatic or biliary cancer, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis
Liver infiltration or abscess, cirrhosis, some drugs (for example flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav)
Bone: Paget disease, fracture healing, osteomalacia, bone metastases, hyperparathyroidism
Growth in childhood and adolescence, third-trimester pregnancy
lower: Hypophosphatasia (rare inherited deficiency)
Hypothyroidism, zinc or magnesium deficiency, malnutrition, some anaemias
factors: Age (children and adolescents), pregnancy, blood group and a recent fatty meal in some people
Fracture healing and bone growth
Sample handling
alp.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

ggt.name: GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase)
ggt.summary: A membrane enzyme of bile-duct and liver cells that rises with cholestasis, alcohol and many medicines. On its own it is too non-specific to diagnose anything, but it confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase comes from the liver rather than bone.
ggt.what: GGT transfers amino acid fragments across cell membranes and is abundant in the biliary tree, liver, kidney and pancreas. Its main practical value is as a companion to ALP: both rise in bile-duct obstruction, whereas ALP alone rises in bone disease and pregnancy. GGT is also induced by alcohol and by enzyme-inducing drugs such as phenytoin and carbamazepine, so a raised GGT with otherwise normal tests often reflects drinking, obesity or medication rather than liver damage. It does not fall quickly after stopping alcohol, taking several weeks to normalise.
higher: Cholestasis of any cause (with ALP)
Alcohol use, especially regular heavy drinking
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes
Enzyme-inducing medicines (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin), some others
Pancreatitis, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
lower: No clinical significance; low in some inherited conditions
factors: Alcohol in the preceding weeks
Medicines
Body weight
Smoking
ggt.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

bilirubin.name: Bilirubin
bilirubin.summary: The yellow pigment made when old red cells are broken down, processed by the liver and excreted in bile. A high level causes jaundice; whether the excess is unconjugated or conjugated tells whether the problem lies before the liver, inside it or in the bile ducts.
bilirubin.what: About 1% of red cells are retired every day, and their haemoglobin is converted into unconjugated bilirubin, which travels bound to albumin to the liver. Hepatocytes attach glucuronic acid to make water-soluble conjugated bilirubin and secrete it into bile, where it gives stools their colour. Excess unconjugated bilirubin means too much production (haemolysis) or slow conjugation (newborns, Gilbert syndrome); excess conjugated bilirubin means damaged hepatocytes or blocked bile ducts, and it spills into urine, turning it dark. Jaundice becomes visible in the whites of the eyes and skin once the total rises above roughly 40 to 50 µmol/L. In newborns very high levels can injure the brain, so bilirubin is monitored closely in the first days of life.
higher: Haemolysis: haemolytic anaemias, transfusion reactions, large bruises (unconjugated)
Gilbert syndrome, a common harmless inherited slowing of conjugation (unconjugated, rises with fasting and illness)
Hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury (mixed)
Bile-duct obstruction by stones, strictures or tumours, primary biliary cholangitis (conjugated)
Newborn jaundice
lower: No clinical significance
factors: Fasting and intercurrent illness raise unconjugated bilirubin in Gilbert syndrome
Haemolysed samples and exposure of the sample to light
Some medicines interfere with the assay or with excretion
bilirubin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

albumin.name: Albumin
albumin.summary: The most abundant protein in blood, made by the liver. It keeps fluid inside the vessels and carries hormones, drugs, calcium and bilirubin. A low level is common in serious illness and reflects inflammation, loss or poor liver synthesis rather than any one disease.
albumin.what: Albumin holds water in the circulation by osmotic pull; when it falls, fluid leaks into tissues and causes oedema and ascites. The liver makes about 10 to 15 grams a day and the protein lasts about three weeks in the circulation, so albumin is a slow measure of synthetic function and falls late in liver disease. Far more often a low albumin reflects the acute-phase response (the liver switches to making inflammatory proteins such as CRP during infection, surgery or cancer), losses through the kidney (nephrotic syndrome) or gut, malnutrition, or dilution by intravenous fluids. Because many drugs and about half of blood calcium ride on albumin, laboratories report a calcium value adjusted for it.
higher: Dehydration (concentration of the blood) is the only common cause of a genuinely high value
lower: Acute and chronic inflammation, infection, sepsis, surgery, cancer
Cirrhosis and other severe liver disease
Nephrotic syndrome (loss in urine), protein-losing enteropathy, burns
Malnutrition and malabsorption
Heart failure, pregnancy, intravenous fluid dilution, older age
factors: Posture (lying down lowers it slightly), tourniquet time and hydration
Acute illness at the time of sampling
Pregnancy
albumin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

creatinine.name: Creatinine
creatinine.summary: A waste product of muscle metabolism produced at a steady rate and cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. The rise in blood creatinine when filtration falls makes it the everyday marker of kidney function and the input for the eGFR calculation.
creatinine.what: Muscle cells store energy as creatine phosphate, and a fixed fraction breaks down each day into creatinine, which the glomeruli filter freely and the tubules barely reabsorb. When the glomerular filtration rate falls, creatinine accumulates, but the relationship is curved: filtration can halve before creatinine leaves the reference interval, and small rises at low values mean large losses of function. Because production depends on muscle mass, a frail older person and a muscular young athlete have different normal values for the same kidney function, which is why laboratories convert creatinine into an estimated GFR that accounts for age and sex. A rising creatinine over hours to days defines acute kidney injury; a persistently reduced eGFR over three months defines chronic kidney disease.
higher: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, shock, obstruction, nephrotoxic drugs, contrast
Chronic kidney disease from diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease and others
Large muscle mass, creatine supplements, a large meat meal, muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis)
Medicines that block tubular secretion without harming the kidney (trimethoprim, cimetidine), and ACE inhibitors or ARBs starting (a small expected rise)
lower: Low muscle mass: older age, frailty, amputation, muscle-wasting disease
Pregnancy (higher filtration), liver disease, malnutrition
factors: Muscle mass, sex, age and ethnicity affect the value for a given filtration rate
Cooked meat, creatine supplements and intense exercise in the previous day
Hydration; some medicines
Assay standardisation between laboratories
creatinine.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management

egfr.name: eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate)
egfr.summary: An estimate of how many millilitres of blood the kidneys filter each minute, calculated from creatinine together with age and sex. The number used to stage chronic kidney disease and to adjust drug doses.
egfr.what: The glomerular filtration rate is the best overall measure of kidney function but cannot be measured directly in routine care, so laboratories estimate it from serum creatinine using equations (the CKD-EPI equation in current UK and US practice; the 2021 version no longer includes a race term) that adjust for age and sex. The result is expressed per 1.73 m² of body surface area. An eGFR persistently below 60 for more than three months, or any value with markers of kidney damage such as albumin in the urine, defines chronic kidney disease, staged from G1 to G5. The estimate is least reliable at extremes of muscle mass, in pregnancy, in acute illness where creatinine is still changing, and near the normal range, where a cystatin C-based estimate can confirm the finding.
higher: A high value is normal in young adults and in pregnancy; falsely high estimates occur with low muscle mass (the equation assumes average muscle)
lower: Chronic kidney disease of any cause (diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidneys, obstruction)
Acute kidney injury (the estimate lags behind the true fall because creatinine takes time to accumulate)
Falsely low with high muscle mass, creatine supplements, a recent meat meal, or drugs that block creatinine secretion
factors: Everything that changes creatinine independently of filtration
Which equation the laboratory uses
Steady-state assumption: the estimate is invalid while kidney function is changing rapidly
egfr.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management
KDIGO 2024 clinical practice guideline for the evaluation and management of chronic kidney disease

urea.name: Urea
urea.summary: The nitrogen-containing waste the liver makes from protein breakdown, cleared by the kidneys. Reported as urea in the UK and as blood urea nitrogen (BUN) in the United States, it rises with kidney impairment but also with dehydration, bleeding into the gut and a high-protein diet.
urea.what: Ammonia released when amino acids are broken down is toxic, so the liver converts it into urea, which the kidneys filter; unlike creatinine, a good deal of urea is reabsorbed in the tubules, and more is reabsorbed when the body is dry. Urea therefore rises out of proportion to creatinine in dehydration, heart failure with poor kidney perfusion and gastrointestinal bleeding (digested blood is a protein load), and it falls in liver failure and malnutrition. Read alongside creatinine, the urea-to-creatinine pattern helps sort out whether a kidney problem is pre-renal (poor blood supply) or intrinsic. Very high urea in advanced kidney failure contributes to the nausea, itching and drowsiness of uraemia.
urea.unit: mmol/L (urea, UK) or mg/dL (BUN, US); urea 1 mmol/L ≈ BUN 2.8 mg/dL
higher: Kidney impairment, acute or chronic
Dehydration, heart failure, shock (reduced kidney perfusion)
Gastrointestinal bleeding, high-protein diet, corticosteroids, tissue breakdown
Urinary obstruction
lower: Severe liver disease (less urea made)
Malnutrition, low-protein diet, pregnancy
Over-hydration; some inherited enzyme defects
factors: Hydration and protein intake
Corticosteroids and tetracyclines
Recent gut bleeding
urea.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

potassium.name: Potassium
potassium.summary: The main positively charged ion inside cells; only about 2% is in the blood, but that small fraction sets the electrical excitability of nerves, muscle and above all the heart. Both high and low levels can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
potassium.what: The kidney matches potassium excretion to intake under the control of aldosterone, and insulin and adrenaline shift potassium into cells, which is why a rapid change in blood level can occur without any change in total body stores. Hyperkalaemia is most often a combination of reduced kidney excretion and medicines that block aldosterone or the renin-angiotensin system (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, potassium supplements); it flattens the heart's electrical recovery and can cause cardiac arrest, so a very high result is treated as an emergency and checked with an ECG. Hypokalaemia comes from losses through vomiting, diarrhoea or loop and thiazide diuretics and causes weakness, cramps and arrhythmias, particularly in people taking digoxin. Because red cells are full of potassium, a squeezed, delayed or haemolysed sample reads falsely high.
higher: Kidney impairment, acute or chronic
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone and other potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, potassium supplements and salt substitutes
Addison disease (aldosterone deficiency)
Tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis), acidosis, insulin deficiency in diabetic ketoacidosis
Spurious: haemolysed or delayed samples, very high platelet or white-cell counts
lower: Vomiting, diarrhoea, laxative misuse
Loop and thiazide diuretics, corticosteroids, high-dose salbutamol, insulin treatment
Low magnesium, Conn syndrome (aldosterone excess), Cushing syndrome
Poor intake, refeeding, alkalosis
factors: Sample handling: fist clenching, tourniquet time, delay before separation, haemolysis
Recent insulin, salbutamol or intravenous fluids
Kidney function and current medicines
potassium.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

sodium.name: Sodium
sodium.summary: The main positively charged ion of the fluid outside cells and the chief determinant of blood osmolality. Its blood level says more about the body's water balance than about salt: a low sodium usually means too much water relative to salt, a high one too little water.
sodium.what: Total body sodium sets the volume of the extracellular fluid, but the concentration in blood is regulated by thirst and by antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which tells the kidney how much water to retain. Hyponatraemia, the commonest electrolyte abnormality in hospital, arises when ADH is released inappropriately (illness, pain, some drugs, lung and brain disease), when thiazide diuretics or adrenal failure waste salt, or when heart, liver or kidney failure retain water in excess of salt. A fall that develops quickly swells brain cells and causes confusion, seizures and coma. Hypernatraemia reflects water loss that has not been replaced (fever, diarrhoea, diabetes insipidus) in people who cannot drink enough, typically the very young, the very old and the unwell. Correction in either direction must be gradual to avoid brain injury.
higher: Water loss without replacement: fever, sweating, diarrhoea, osmotic diuresis in uncontrolled diabetes, diabetes insipidus
Inability to drink: infancy, dementia, unconsciousness
Excess salt intake or hypertonic fluids (rare)
lower: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH): lung and brain disease, cancers, pain, nausea, medicines such as SSRIs, carbamazepine, antipsychotics
Thiazide diuretics
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (dilution)
Adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism
Excess water intake, prolonged endurance exercise with water only
Spurious (pseudohyponatraemia) with very high lipids or proteins, or a sample drawn near a drip
factors: Fluid intake and intravenous fluids at the time of sampling
Glucose: very high blood glucose lowers the measured sodium
Medicines, especially diuretics and antidepressants
sodium.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

tsh.name: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
tsh.summary: The pituitary hormone that drives the thyroid gland. Because the pituitary responds to tiny changes in thyroid hormone, TSH moves in the opposite direction to thyroid function and is the single most sensitive test of thyroid status.
tsh.what: The hypothalamus releases TRH, the pituitary responds with TSH, and TSH tells the thyroid to make thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); T4 and T3 then feed back to switch TSH off. When the thyroid fails, T4 falls and TSH climbs, often to many times the upper limit; when the thyroid is overactive, TSH is suppressed towards zero. The relationship is logarithmic, so TSH changes a great deal for a small change in T4, which is why it is the screening test and the value used to adjust levothyroxine. It takes about six weeks to settle after a dose change. TSH is unreliable when the pituitary itself is diseased, in the recovery phase of severe illness, and in the first trimester of pregnancy, when the placental hormone hCG mimics it.
higher: Primary hypothyroidism: autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, after thyroid surgery or radioiodine, iodine deficiency
Under-replacement with levothyroxine, or poor absorption of it (taken with food, iron, calcium, PPIs)
Subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH with normal free T4)
Recovery from severe illness, some medicines (amiodarone, lithium), rarely a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour
lower: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules, thyroiditis
Over-replacement with levothyroxine
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease (secondary hypothyroidism: low TSH with low T4)
First trimester of pregnancy, severe non-thyroidal illness, high-dose steroids and dopamine
factors: Time of day (highest overnight), acute illness, pregnancy
Biotin supplements interfere with some assays
Levothyroxine dose timing and adherence
Age: the reference interval rises in older adults
tsh.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG145: Thyroid disease: assessment and management

free-t4.name: Free T4 (thyroxine)
free-t4.summary: The unbound fraction of thyroxine, the main hormone the thyroid gland secretes. Measured with TSH, it tells whether a thyroid problem is mild or severe and whether it originates in the thyroid or the pituitary.
free-t4.what: The thyroid releases mostly T4, with a smaller amount of the more active T3; tissues convert T4 to T3 as needed. Over 99% of T4 travels bound to carrier proteins, so laboratories measure the free fraction, which is what acts on cells and is not distorted by pregnancy or the pill, both of which raise the binding proteins. A low free T4 with a high TSH is primary hypothyroidism; a low free T4 with a low or normal TSH points to pituitary disease; a high free T4 with a suppressed TSH is hyperthyroidism. Free T4 changes more quickly than TSH after starting or adjusting treatment and is the value followed in pituitary disease, where TSH cannot be trusted.
higher: Hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre, thyroiditis)
Excess levothyroxine
Amiodarone, heparin (assay effect), biotin interference, acute psychiatric illness (transient)
Rare TSH-secreting pituitary tumours or thyroid hormone resistance
lower: Primary hypothyroidism
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease
Severe non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid pattern), some antiepileptic drugs and high-dose steroids
Under-treatment or malabsorption of levothyroxine
factors: Timing of the levothyroxine dose (a sample soon after a dose reads higher)
Biotin and some antibodies interfere with immunoassays
Severe illness, pregnancy (trimester-specific ranges)
free-t4.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

references.title: NICE NG145: Thyroid disease: assessment and management

crp.name: C-reactive protein (CRP)
crp.summary: A protein the liver pours into blood within hours of any significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury. It rises and falls fast, so it tracks the course of an illness and the response to treatment; it does not say what the cause is.
crp.what: CRP is an acute-phase protein: interleukin-6 released at a site of inflammation tells the liver to make it, levels begin to rise within about six hours, peak at around two days and fall with a half-life of roughly 19 hours once the trigger is removed. Bacterial infection, major surgery, trauma, heart attack, flares of inflammatory arthritis or bowel disease and some cancers all raise it, often into the hundreds of mg/L; many viral infections and some autoimmune diseases such as lupus raise it only modestly. A high-sensitivity assay (hs-CRP) measures the low-grade inflammation of obesity and atherosclerosis, used in some cardiovascular risk scores. CRP responds faster than the ESR, which is why it is preferred for monitoring acute illness.
higher: Bacterial infection, sepsis, abscess, pneumonia, pyelonephritis
Surgery, trauma, burns, myocardial infarction
Inflammatory arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, vasculitis, gout flares
Cancer, particularly lymphoma and widespread disease
Mild elevation: obesity, smoking, diabetes, low-grade chronic inflammation
lower: A low value is normal; it makes significant bacterial infection or major inflammation less likely but does not exclude early infection, viral illness or localised infection
factors: Time since the illness began (a sample within the first hours can be normal)
Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants blunt the rise
Obesity and smoking raise the baseline
Pregnancy and oestrogens raise it slightly
crp.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

ferritin.name: Ferritin
ferritin.summary: The protein that stores iron inside cells; the small amount in blood mirrors the body's iron reserve. A low ferritin is the most reliable single sign of iron deficiency, but because ferritin is also an acute-phase protein, inflammation can hide a deficiency by pushing it into the normal range.
ferritin.what: Most of the body's iron is in haemoglobin, and the rest is held in the liver, spleen and bone marrow wrapped in ferritin. Serum ferritin falls as those stores are drained, before the haemoglobin drops, so it detects iron deficiency at an early stage; a value below about 30 µg/L confirms depleted stores in an adult. Ferritin rises with inflammation, infection, liver disease, cancer and alcohol whether or not iron is present, so in someone with a raised CRP a 'normal' ferritin can still coexist with deficiency, and transferrin saturation or a trial of iron may be needed. Very high ferritin points to iron overload (haemochromatosis, repeated transfusions) or to severe inflammatory states.
higher: Inflammation and infection (acute-phase response), rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease
Liver disease, alcohol excess, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Haemochromatosis and iron overload from transfusions
Cancer, especially lymphoma and leukaemia; very high values in adult Still disease and haemophagocytic syndromes
Metabolic syndrome, obesity
lower: Iron deficiency from blood loss (menstrual, gastrointestinal), poor intake, malabsorption (coeliac disease, gastric surgery), pregnancy and growth
Hypothyroidism and vitamin C deficiency (small effect)
factors: Any concurrent inflammation raises it independently of iron stores
Time of day, alcohol, liver disease
Recent iron infusion or transfusion
ferritin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.
